questions.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,4,4)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,4,4)=-\frac{2}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{108}, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{y}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{z}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,4,4)=-\frac{4}{{({2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{4}^{2})}^{3/2}}=-\frac{1}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,4,4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,4,4) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,4,4),{f}_{y}(2,4,4),{f}_{z}(2,4,4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,4,4)+∇f(2,4,4)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}+⟨-\frac{1}{108},-\frac{1}{54},-\frac{1}{54}⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-4,z-4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{108}(x-2)-\frac{1}{54}(y-4)-\frac{1}{54}(z-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{x}{108}+\frac{1}{54}-\frac{y}{54}+\frac{4}{54}-\frac{z}{54}+\frac{4}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x}{108}-\frac{y}{54}-\frac{z}{54}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(\frac{\pi }{2},2)+∇f(\frac{\pi }{2},2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{\pi }{2},y-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(\frac{\pi }{2},2)=0.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\, & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{2},2)=(2)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2)=-4, \\ {f}_{y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},2)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2)+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2)=-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(\frac{\pi }{2},2) & =⟨-4,-\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(\frac{\pi }{2},2)+∇\,f(\frac{\pi }{2},2)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{\pi }{2},\,y-2⟩ \\  & =0+⟨-4,-\pi ⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{\pi }{2},\,y-2⟩ \\  & =-4(x-\frac{\pi }{2})-\pi (y-2) \\  & =4\pi -4x-\pi y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y,z)$ is a differentiable function such that

$$
f(2,-2,-1)=4,\,{f}_{x}(2,-2,-1)=2,\,{f}_{y}(2,-2,-1)=-2,\,{f}_{z}(2,-2,-1)=-4.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,-2,-1)$ estimate the value of $f(2.02,-1.98,-1.05)$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,-2,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,-2,-1)+∇f(2,-2,-1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y+2,z+1⟩ \\  & =f(2,-2,-1)+⟨{f}_{x}(2,-2,-1),{f}_{y}(2,-2,-1),{f}_{z}(2,-2,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y+2,z+1⟩ \\  & =4+⟨2,-2,-4⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y+2,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(2.02,-1.98,-1.05)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=2.02,$ $y=-1.98,$ and $z=-1.05$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.02,-1.98,-1.05) & ≈4+⟨2,-2,-4⟩\cdot ⟨2.02-2,-1.98+2,-1.05+1⟩ \\  & =4+⟨2,-2,-4⟩\cdot ⟨0.02,0.02,-0.05⟩ \\  & =4+(0.04-0.04+0.2) \\  & =4.2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x,y,z)$ is a differentiable function such that

$$
f(3,0,4)=-5,\,{f}_{x}(3,0,4)=3,\,{f}_{y}(3,0,4)=-1,\,{f}_{z}(3,0,4)=2.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3,0,4)$ estimate the value of $f(2.97,-0.02,3.98).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3,0,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(3,0,4)+∇f(3,0,4)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-0,z-4⟩ \\  & =f(3,0,4)+⟨{f}_{x}(3,0,4),{f}_{y}(3,0,4),{f}_{z}(3,0,4)⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y,z-4⟩ \\  & =-5+⟨3,-1,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y,z-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(2.97,-0.02,3.98)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=2.97,$ $y=-0.02,$ and $z=3.98$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.97,-0.02,3.98) & ≈-5+⟨3,-1,2⟩\cdot ⟨2.97-3,-0.02,3.98-4⟩ \\  & =-5+⟨3,-1,2⟩\cdot ⟨-0.03,-0.02,-0.02⟩ \\  & =-5-0.09+0.02-0.04 \\  & =-5.11\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,-1,-1)=-1,\,{f}_{x}(x,y,z)=2x,\,{f}_{y}(x,y,z)=-2z,\,{f}_{z}(x,y,z)=-2y.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1,-1),$ estimate the value of $f(1.01,-1.02,-1.03).$
questions.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,-1,-1)+∇f(1,-1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-(-1),z-(-1)⟩ \\  & ≈-1+⟨{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1),{f}_{y}(1,-1,-1),{f}_{z}(1,-1,-1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,-1,-1),$ ${f}_{y}(1,-1,-1)$ and ${f}_{z}(1,-1,-1),$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-1,-1) & =2(1)=2 \\ {f}_{y}(1,-1,-1) & =-2(-1)=2 \\ {f}_{z}(1,-1,-1) & =-2(-1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y,z)≈-1+⟨2,2,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+1,z+1⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(1.01,-1.02,-1.03)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.01,y=-1.02$ and $z=-1.03,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.01,-1.02,-1.03) & ≈-1+⟨2,2,2⟩\cdot ⟨1.01-1,-1.02+1,-1.03+1⟩ \\  & ≈-1+⟨2,2,2⟩\cdot ⟨0.01,-0.02,-0.03⟩ \\  & ≈-1+2(0.01)+2(-0.02)+2(-0.03) \\  & ≈-1+0.02-0.04-0.06 \\  & ≈-1.08\end{aligned}
$$
